title: Neurological Biomarker Analysis Reveals Smoking-Related GFAP Alterations Independent of Sleep Apnea
content: Background: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and smoking are associated with oxidative stress, neuronal damage and cardiovascular risk. This study investigated whether subclinical sleep apnea (SSA) - undiagnosed sleep-disordered breathing - or smoking exposure and nicotine dependence are associated with serum glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and neurofilament light chain (NfL) levels in young, healthy adults. Method: This cross-sectional analysis included 1,125 participants from the population-based GAPP cohort (mean age 34.4 years; 51.8% female). SSA was defined as an oxygen desaturation index (ODI; number of ≥4% oxygen desaturations per hour) and/or a respiratory event index (REI; number of apneas and hypopneas per hour) of ≥5. Smoking exposure and nicotine dependence was assessed by smoking years, pack-years, and the Fagerström Test for Nicotine Dependence (FTND). Associations with serum GFAP and NfL levels were investigated using ANCOVA models adjusted for relevant confounders. Results: SSA was present in 4.5% of participants. Current and former smoking prevalence were 20.8% and 22%, respectively. GFAP levels were higher among participants with SSA, but neither GFAP nor NfL was significantly associated with SSA. In contrast, smoking exposure and nicotine dependence were inversely associated with GFAP concentrations, with smoking years remaining significant across adjusted models, whereas NfL levels showed no significant associations with smoking measures. Conclusion: In young, healthy adults, SSA was not associated with GFAP or NfL levels, whereas smoking measures were independently associated with lower GFAP concentrations but not with NfL levels, suggesting smoking-related biological processes may affect astrocytic and axonal biomarkers differently in early adulthood.
